results.title: Support of the prime exponents of a fractional ideal
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$. For a unit fractional ideal $I$ of $R$ in $K$, this is the finite set of height-one primes $v$ of $R$ at which the $v$-adic valuation of $I$ is nonzero.

results.title: Prime exponents of an invertible fractional ideal
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$, and let $I$ be a unit of the monoid of fractional ideals of $R$ in $K$. The prime exponents of $I$ form the finitely supported function from the height-one primes of $R$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ that sends each height-one prime $v$ to the exponent $\operatorname{ord}_v(I)$ of $v$ in the factorization $I = \prod_v v^{\operatorname{ord}_v(I)}$; its support is the finite…

results.title: Products of prime powers are nonzero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$. For every finitely supported function $e$ from the height-one primes of $R$ to $\mathbb{Z}$, the fractional ideal $\prod_v v^{e(v)}$ of $R$ in $K$, the product over the primes $v$ with $e(v) \neq 0$, is nonzero.

results.title: Fractional ideal with prescribed prime exponents
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$. For a finitely supported function $e$ from the height-one primes of $R$ to $\mathbb{Z}$, this is the fractional ideal $\prod_v v^{e(v)}$ of $R$ in $K$, the product over the primes $v$ with $e(v) \neq 0$, regarded as a unit of the monoid of fractional ideals (it is nonzero, hence invertible).

results.title: Valuations of a product of prime powers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$. For every finitely supported function $e$ from the height-one primes of $R$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ and every height-one prime $v$ of $R$, the $v$-adic valuation of the fractional ideal $\prod_w w^{e(w)}$, the product over the primes $w$ with $e(w) \neq 0$, equals $e(v)$.

results.title: Reconstructing a fractional ideal from its prime exponents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$, and for a unit fractional ideal $I$ of $R$ in $K$ and a height-one prime $v$ of $R$ write $\operatorname{val}_v(I)$ for the $v$-adic valuation of $I$. Every unit fractional ideal $I$ of $R$ in $K$ equals $\prod_v v^{\operatorname{val}_v(I)}$, the product over the height-one primes $v$ of $R$ with $\operatorname{val}_v(I) \neq 0$.

results.title: Recovering prime exponents from a product of prime powers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$, and let $e$ be a finitely supported function from the height-one primes of $R$ to $\mathbb{Z}$. The prime-exponent function of the fractional ideal $\prod_w w^{e(w)}$, the product over the primes $w$ with $e(w) \neq 0$, is $e$: its $v$-adic valuation is $e(v)$ for every height-one prime $v$ of $R$.

results.title: Prime exponents are additive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$, and for a unit fractional ideal $I$ of $R$ in $K$ and a height-one prime $v$ of $R$ write $\operatorname{val}_v(I)$ for the $v$-adic valuation of $I$. For all unit fractional ideals $I$ and $J$ of $R$ in $K$ and every height-one prime $v$ of $R$, $\operatorname{val}_v(IJ) = \operatorname{val}_v(I) + \operatorname{val}_v(J)$.

results.title: Prime factorization isomorphism for fractional ideals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$, and for a unit fractional ideal $I$ of $R$ in $K$ and a height-one prime $v$ of $R$ write $\operatorname{val}_v(I)$ for the $v$-adic valuation of $I$. results.title: Exponent function of a prime ideal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$ and let $w$ be a height-one prime of $R$. The factorization isomorphism sends the fractional ideal $w$, as a unit fractional ideal of $R$ in $K$, to the function on height-one primes of $R$ that is $1$ at $w$ and $0$ elsewhere.

results.title: Inverse factorization of a single prime power
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$, let $w$ be a height-one prime of $R$ and let $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. The inverse of the factorization isomorphism sends the function on height-one primes of $R$ that is $n$ at $w$ and $0$ elsewhere to the fractional ideal $w^n$.

results.title: Finitely many primes contain a nonzero element
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a Dedekind domain $A$, every nonzero element $a$ lies in only finitely many prime ideals of $A$.

results.title: Finitely many primes contain a nonzero ideal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a Dedekind domain $A$, every nonzero ideal $I$ is contained in only finitely many prime ideals of $A$.

results.title: Vanishing multiplicity of a prime factor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain, let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal of $A$ and let $I$ be a nonzero ideal of $A$. Then the multiplicity of $\mathfrak p$ in the factorization of $I$ into prime ideals is zero if and only if $I \not\subseteq \mathfrak p$.

results.title: Fractional ideals have finite support
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain with field of fractions $K$, and let $I$ be a fractional ideal of $A$ in $K$. For a nonzero prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ of $A$, let $v_{\mathfrak p}(I) \in \mathbb Z$ be the exponent of $\mathfrak p$ in the factorization of $I$ into prime ideals, with $v_{\mathfrak p}(0) = 0$. Then $v_{\mathfrak p}(I) \neq 0$ for only finitely many nonzero prime ideals $\mathfrak p$ of $A$.

Then for every ideal $I$ of $R$, the multiplicity of $\mathfrak m$ in the extended ideal $I R_{\mathfrak p}$ equals the multiplicity of $\mathfrak p$ in $I$. results.title: Atomless measure
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A measure $\mu$ on a measurable space is atomless when every measurable set $s$ with $\mu(s) > 0$ contains a measurable subset $t \subseteq s$ with $0 < \mu(t) < \mu(s)$.

results.title: Restriction of an atomless measure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The restriction of an atomless measure to a measurable set is atomless.

results.title: Sierpiński's theorem on atomless measures
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite atomless measure. For every measurable set $s$ and every $t \in [0, \infty]$ with $t \le \mu(s)$, there is a measurable set $u \subseteq s$ with $\mu(u) = t$.

results.title: Atomless measures have null singletons
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If `μ` is atomless and singletons are measurable, then every singleton is `μ`-null (`NullSingletonClass`): a singleton of positive measure would contain a measurable subset of strictly smaller positive measure, but its only subsets are `∅` and itself.

results.title: Convex functions of martingales are submartingales

Let $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex, and suppose $\varphi(X_n)$ is integrable for every $n$. Then $(\varphi(X_n))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a submartingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$.

part.title: Heap semantics of IMP
api: Modified variables of a heap command

results.title: Heap
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A heap is a finite partial map from addresses to values, where addresses and values are natural numbers: it stores a value $v \in \mathbb{N}$ at each address of a finite set of addresses in $\mathbb{N}$, called the addresses allocated in the heap.

results.title: Disjoint heaps
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint when no address is allocated in both: every address allocated in $h_1$ is not allocated in $h_2$.

results.title: Symmetry of heap disjointness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, if $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint, then $h_2$ and $h_1$ are disjoint.

results.title: The empty heap is disjoint from every heap
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every heap $h$, the empty heap is disjoint from $h$ (with the empty heap as the first heap).

results.title: Every heap is disjoint from the empty heap
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every heap $h$, $h$ is disjoint from the empty heap (with the empty heap as the second heap).

results.title: Erasing an address that the right heap of a union lacks
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, let $h_1 \cup h_2$ be their left-biased union (at an address allocated in both it keeps the value from $h_1$). If the address $a$ is not allocated in $h_2$, then erasing $a$ from $h_1 \cup h_2$ gives the union of $h_2$ with the heap obtained from $h_1$ by erasing $a$, taken with that heap on the left.

results.title: Inserting an address the other heap lacks preserves disjointness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint and the address $a$ is not allocated in $h_2$, then for every value $v$, the heap obtained from $h_1$ by inserting $a$ with value $v$ (overwriting any value $h_1$ stores at $a$) is disjoint from $h_2$.

results.title: Erasing an address preserves disjointness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint, then for every address $a$, the heap obtained from $h_1$ by erasing $a$ (removing the address $a$ and its value) is disjoint from $h_2$.

results.title: Disjointness from a singleton heap
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every address $a$, value $v$ and heap $h$, the singleton heap that stores $v$ at $a$ and allocates no other address is disjoint from $h$ if and only if $a$ is not allocated in $h$.

results.title: Reinserting an erased value restores the heap
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a heap $h$ stores the value $v$ at the address $a$, then erasing $a$ from $h$ and then inserting $a$ with value $v$ gives back $h$.

results.title: Every heap has a free address
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every heap $h$ there is an address that is not allocated in $h$.

results.title: Heap commands
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: Heap commands extend the commands of IMP with heap operations. A heap command is one of: $\mathbf{skip}$; an assignment $x := a$; a sequence $c_1; c_2$; a conditional $\mathbf{if}\ b\ \mathbf{then}\ c_1\ \mathbf{else}\ c_2$; a loop $\mathbf{while}\ b\ \mathbf{do}\ c$; a heap read $x := [a]$; a heap write $[a] := e$; an allocation $x := \mathbf{alloc}(e)$; or a deallocation $\mathbf{free}(a)$. Here $x$ is a variable…

results.title: Heap configurations
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A heap configuration is a triple $(c, s, h)$ of a heap command $c$, a store $s$ and a heap $h$.

results.title: Small-step semantics of heap commands
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The single-step relation $(c, s, h) \to (c', s', h')$ on heap configurations is the least relation closed under the rules below. Here $a(s)$ is the value of an expression $a$ in the store $s$, $s[x \mapsto n]$ is $s$ with variable $x$ set to $n$, $h[\ell \mapsto n]$ is $h$ with address $\ell$ set to $n$, and $h \setminus \ell$ is $h$ with address $\ell$ removed.

results.title: Multi-step heap execution
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The relation $(c, s, h) \to^* (c', s', h')$ on heap configurations is the reflexive-transitive closure of the small-step relation: it holds when the first configuration reaches the second by a finite, possibly empty, sequence of small steps.

results.title: Safe heap configurations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A heap configuration, consisting of a heap command, a store and a heap, is safe when every heap configuration reachable from it in zero or more heap steps either has command $\mathtt{skip}$ or can take a further heap step.

results.title: Safety is preserved along executions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a heap configuration is safe and reaches a second configuration by finitely many (possibly zero) small steps, then the second configuration is safe.

results.title: Adding a frame heap preserves the ability to step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps, $c$ a heap command and $s$ a store. If the configuration $(c, s, h)$ can take a small step, then so can $(c, s, h \cup h_f)$.

results.title: Frame decomposition of a single heap step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps, $c$ a heap command and $s$ a store, and suppose that the configuration $(c, s, h)$ can take a small step. If $(c, s, h \cup h_f)$ takes a small step to $(c', s', h'')$, then there is a heap $h_1$, disjoint from $h_f$, such that $(c, s, h)$ takes a small step to $(c', s', h_1)$ and $h'' = h_1 \cup h_f$.

results.title: Frame decomposition of heap executions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps, $c$ a heap command and $s$ a store, and suppose that the configuration $(c, s, h)$ is safe. If $(c, s, h \cup h_f)$ reaches $(c'', s'', h'')$ by finitely many (possibly zero) small steps, then there is a heap $h_2$, disjoint from $h_f$, such that $(c, s, h)$ reaches $(c'', s'', h_2)$ by finitely many small steps, $h'' = h_2 \cup h_f$, and $(c'', s'', h_2)$ is safe.

results.title: Embedding of IMP into the heap language
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The embedding sends each plain IMP command to the heap command of the same shape: $\mathtt{skip}$ goes to $\mathtt{skip}$, an assignment of an arithmetic expression to a variable goes to the same assignment, a sequence goes to the sequence of the embeddings of its parts, and a conditional or while loop goes to the conditional or while loop with the same guard and with each subcommand replaced by its embedding.

results.title: Heap steps of embedded commands are plain steps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ be a plain IMP command, $s$ a store and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$ into the heap language. Then $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ takes a heap step to a heap configuration $K$ if and only if there are a plain command $c'$ and a store $s'$ such that $(c, s)$ takes a plain small step to $(c', s')$ and $K = (\overline{c'}, s', h)$.

results.title: Executions of embedded commands are plain executions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ be a plain IMP command, $s$ a store and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$ into the heap language. If $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches a heap configuration $(c_2, s_2, h_2)$ in zero or more heap steps, then $h_2 = h$ and there is a plain command $c_2'$ with $c_2 = \overline{c_2'}$ such that $(c, s)$ reaches $(c_2', s_2)$ in zero or more plain small steps.

results.title: Plain executions lift to the heap language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c, c_2$ be plain IMP commands, $s, s_2$ stores and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$ into the heap language. If $(c, s)$ reaches $(c_2, s_2)$ in zero or more plain small steps, then $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches $(\overline{c_2}, s_2, h)$ in zero or more heap steps.

results.title: Embedded plain commands are safe
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every plain IMP command $c$ with embedding $\overline{c}$ into the heap language, every store $s$ and every heap $h$, the heap configuration $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ is safe.

results.title: Embedding preserves termination
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ be a plain IMP command with embedding $\overline{c}$ into the heap language, let $s, s'$ be stores and let $h$ be a heap. Then $c$ terminates from $s$ with final store $s'$ if and only if $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches $(\mathtt{skip}, s', h)$ in zero or more heap steps.

results.title: Modified variables of a heap command
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The set $\mathrm{mod}(c)$ of variables a heap command $c$ may assign to is defined by recursion on $c$. It is empty for $\mathbf{skip}$, a heap write $[a] := e$ and a deallocation $\mathbf{free}(a)$; it is $\{x\}$ for an assignment $x := a$, a heap read $x := [a]$ and an allocation $x := \mathbf{alloc}(e)$; it is $\mathrm{mod}(c_1) \cup \mathrm{mod}(c_2)$ for a sequence $c_1; c_2$ and for a conditional…

results.title: Steps do not enlarge the modified variables
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $\mathrm{mod}(c)$ for the set of variables a heap command $c$ may assign to. If the configuration $(c, s, h)$ takes a small step to $(c', s', h')$, then $\mathrm{mod}(c') \subseteq \mathrm{mod}(c)$.

results.title: A heap step only changes assignable variables
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a heap configuration $(c, s, h)$ takes one heap step to $(c', s', h')$, then $s'(x) = s(x)$ for every variable $x$ outside the set of variables that $c$ may assign to.

results.title: Heap executions only change assignable variables
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a heap configuration $(c, s, h)$ reaches a heap configuration $(c', s', h')$ in zero or more heap steps, then $s'(x) = s(x)$ for every variable $x$ outside the set of variables that $c$ may assign to.
